info.name: Beta Platform — Integration API (v1)
info.description:
Integration API for the Beta Platform: sign in for a bearer token, renew it with a refresh token, read and add products, and raise a work order.

## Start here
1. Set `baseUrl` (default `http://localhost:5045`, the app's default launch profile).
2. Set `adminEmail` / `adminPassword`.
3. Run **1 · Auth → Sign in**. It stores `{{accessToken}}` and `{{refreshToken}}`.
4. Run **2 · Products → List products** and **2b · Machines → List machines**. Between them they pick real product codes and a real machine id out of your database and store them, so the work-order requests below run against your data rather than against values invented here.
5. When the access token expires, run **Renew tokens** instead of signing in again.

Access tokens last **8 hours**; refresh tokens last **30 days** and are **rotated** on every renewal — the response always carries a new one, and the old one should be discarded.

## Every protected request shows its token
Each authenticated request carries its own `Authorization: Bearer {{accessToken}}` header, spelled out on the request rather than inherited from the collection. It is the same credential either way; stating it means you can read any single request and see exactly what it sends. `POST /auth/login`, `POST /auth/refresh` and the OpenAPI document are the only anonymous calls.

## Products are addressed by CODE — machines by id
No **product** record number appears anywhere in this API, in either direction. `GET /machines` is the deliberate exception: a machine has no external code on this surface, and `machineId` is what a work order has to name, so that endpoint returns it. A work order names its input and output products by the code the plant prints and files by — **several inputs, one output**: `inputProductCodes` is a list (at least one entry, none blank, no code twice), `outputProductCode` is a single code. An unresolvable input is answered by a 400 naming its position, `inputProductCodes[i]`, and if several entries are wrong they are all named in the same response.

## What the folders are for
**0–3** are the seven operations on their happy paths, in the order you would run them. **4 · Refusals** exercises the failures deliberately — an unknown code, a duplicate code, a duplicate order number, a deactivated product. They are separated so that **Run collection** stays predictable, and they depend on 1–3 having run first in the same session.

Live document: `{{baseUrl}}/openapi/v1.json` · Interactive reference: `{{baseUrl}}/docs`

item.name: 1 · Auth
item.description: A real account, a real password check, a real token.

request.description: Anonymous — the password is the credential. Stores both tokens as collection variables. The access token lasts 8 hours; when it expires run **Renew tokens** rather than sending the password again.

request.description:
Exchanges the refresh token for a fresh pair — no password, and no access token required (the caller's may well have expired, which is the point).

Renewal **rotates**: the response carries a new refresh token and this request stores it over the old one. Roles and the account's active state are re-read from the platform, so a deactivated account or a changed password stops renewals immediately rather than at the 30-day expiry.

item.name: 2 · Products
item.description: The stored catalogue. Reads come from the products table; a created product is stored and appears on the platform's own Products screen.

item.name: List products  ▶ saves real codes for the requests below

header.description: The token stored by Sign in. Stated here rather than inherited, so the request shows what it sends.

request.description:
Any authenticated caller. The whole stored catalogue; an empty catalogue is `[]`, never a 404. Enable the `activeOnly` query parameter to exclude deactivated products.

Its test script stores two active codes and one output code, so the work-order requests below run against products that actually exist in your database.

// May legitimately repeat an input: a rework order consumes and produces the same product.

request.description:
Addressed by product code. Codes are trimmed and matched case-insensitively, so `rm-steel-01` and `  RM-Steel-01  ` reach the same product.

A **deactivated** product is returned here, marked `isActive: false`, rather than reported missing — "never existed" and "no longer used" are different answers, and a caller reconciling history needs to tell them apart.

item.name: 2b · Machines
item.description:
The fleet, with ids.

This is the one place the API returns a record id, and it is deliberate: a product has an external identity — the code the plant prints — so its record number is a detail a caller must never need, while a machine has no such code on this surface and `machineId` is exactly what **3 · Work orders** asks for.

header.description: The token stored by Sign in.

request.description:
Any authenticated caller. Every machine with its full detail: `machineId`, code, name, its type (id, Arabic and English names, production line), the stored `isActive` and `isRunning` flags, the live `runningState`, and when it was created. An empty fleet is `[]`, never a 404.

**`isRunning` is not `runningState`.** The first is a stored administrator flag; the second is the live state, by the same rule every screen uses — an in-progress work order forces `Running`, otherwise the latest telemetry reading decides, and a machine that has never reported or whose reading has gone stale is `Stopped`, because silence means not producing. `Unknown` survives only for a fresh reading whose status cannot be interpreted.

Its test script stores the first active machine's id in `{{machineId}}`, which **3 · Work orders** then sends.

item.name: 3 · Work orders
item.description: The feature's end goal: an order whose inputs and output are named by product code — a list of input codes, one output code — resolved against the real catalogue and stored.

header.description: Admin or Client. Any other authenticated account is refused with 403.

request.description:
Admin or Client. Inputs are a LIST of product codes (at least one, none blank, no repeats); the output is a single code. Every code is resolved against the stored catalogue before anything is written, so a refused order stores **nothing**.

`machineId` is the one internal identifier that remains one — machines have no external code on this surface. It is filled in by **2b · Machines → List machines**; the field is optional, so you can also remove it.

Run **2 · Products → List products** first so the codes below point at products you actually have.

The order appears on the Work Orders screen in status Ready, and its Details page lists every input product.

item.name: 4 · Refusals
item.description:
The failures, exercised on purpose. Each one depends on folders 1–3 having run in this session: they reuse the token, the product code that was just created, and the work-order number that was just used.

These are the outcomes the contract specified from the start. They are now produced by real stored data rather than documented against a catalogue that did not exist.

request.description: A code no product carries. 404 with a ProblemDetails body — the addressed resource does not exist.

request.description:
Re-sends the code **2 · Products → Create product** just stored, padded with spaces to show that padding is not part of a code's identity.

409, not 400: the request is perfectly well formed, the stored data disagrees with it. A caller branches on the code and retries with a different one rather than hunting its payload for a formatting mistake.

Run Create product first, or this sends an empty code and gets a 400 instead.

exec: pm.test('not reported as a malformed request', () =>

item.name: Unresolvable input code → 400 naming the position

request.description:
Three codes that resolve to nothing — two inputs and the output. 400, **not** 404: the endpoint is not missing, the body is wrong.

The response names every offending entry at once, by its submitted position: `inputProductCodes[1]`, `inputProductCodes[2]`, `outputProductCode`. A caller with a list of materials has to be told which entry to fix — and told about all of them in one round trip rather than three.

Nothing is stored.

item.name: No token → 401 (never a redirect to the login page)

request.description:
The same request as **List products** with its `Authorization` header removed.

A bare 401 — not a 302 to `/Auth/Login`. That is the whole reason bearer is registered as an additional, non-default scheme and named explicitly on each API controller: the browser screens keep their cookie sign-in, and an unauthenticated API call gets an answer a machine can act on.
